text: Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for everyone six months and older as the most effective protection against seasonal flu. The vaccine is updated each year to match circulating strains, and immunity develops about two weeks after vaccination. Adults over 65 may benefit from a high-dose formulation. Side effects are typically mild, including soreness at the injection site, low-grade fever, and fatigue lasting one to two days. The vaccine cannot cause influenza infection because it does not contain live virus.

Hand hygiene remains the single most effective measure to prevent the spread of infectious disease in community settings. Wash hands with soap and warm water for at least 20 seconds before eating, after using the bathroom, after handling raw food, and after coughing or sneezing. When soap and water are unavailable, alcohol-based hand sanitiser containing at least 60% alcohol is an acceptable alternative. Cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue or the inside of the elbow.

Regular physical activity reduces the risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, several cancers, depression, and premature mortality. Adults should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week, or 75 minutes of vigorous activity, plus muscle-strengthening on two or more days. Even small increases in daily movement, such as taking stairs or walking during phone calls, contribute meaningfully to health outcomes.

Healthy eating patterns emphasise vegetables, fruits, whole grains, lean proteins, and unsaturated fats. Limit added sugars to less than 10% of daily calories and sodium to 2,300 milligrams per day. Drinking water rather than sugar-sweetened beverages reduces calorie intake and supports dental health. There is no single diet that works for everyone; sustainable changes that fit personal preferences and cultural traditions are most likely to last.

Adults under 65 should aim for 7 to 9 hours of sleep per night. Consistent sleep and wake times, even on weekends, reinforce the body's circadian rhythm. Avoid caffeine after early afternoon, limit alcohol before bedtime, and keep the bedroom cool, dark, and quiet. Screen use within an hour of bedtime is associated with longer time to fall asleep. Persistent insomnia or excessive daytime sleepiness warrants discussion with a primary care provider.

Sun protection reduces the risk of skin cancer and premature skin ageing. Apply broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher to exposed skin 15 minutes before going outdoors, and reapply every two hours or after swimming. Wear wide-brimmed hats and UV-blocking sunglasses, and seek shade during peak ultraviolet hours from 10am to 4pm. Avoid indoor tanning beds, which are classified as a known human carcinogen.

Smoking cessation produces measurable health benefits within hours of quitting. Heart rate and blood pressure normalise within 20 minutes; carbon monoxide levels drop within 12 hours; circulation and lung function improve within weeks. Risk of heart attack falls by half within one year. Combining nicotine replacement therapy or prescription medications with behavioural support roughly doubles the probability of long-term success.

Routine childhood immunisation protects against measles, mumps, rubella, polio, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, hepatitis B, varicella, and other infections. Vaccines undergo extensive safety review before licensing and continuous monitoring afterwards. Most reactions are minor and short-lived. Falling vaccination rates have led to resurgence of preventable diseases in several countries; community immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons.

Blood pressure should be checked at least once every two years for adults with normal readings, more often for those with elevated readings or risk factors. Lifestyle measures that lower blood pressure include reducing dietary sodium, maintaining a healthy weight, increasing physical activity, limiting alcohol, and managing stress. When lifestyle measures are insufficient, several classes of antihypertensive medication are safe and effective.

Adults should be screened for type 2 diabetes starting at age 35, or earlier if overweight or with additional risk factors. Screening uses fasting blood glucose, haemoglobin A1c, or oral glucose tolerance testing. Early detection allows lifestyle changes and, if needed, medication to prevent or delay complications including cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, and vision loss.

Colorectal cancer screening is recommended for average-risk adults starting at age 45. Options include colonoscopy every 10 years, faecal immunochemical testing annually, stool DNA testing every three years, or CT colonography every five years. Screening reduces colorectal cancer mortality by identifying precancerous polyps that can be removed before becoming malignant.

Mammographic screening for breast cancer is offered to women starting between ages 40 and 50, with continued screening every one to two years. Discuss benefits, limitations, and personal risk factors with a primary care provider. Self-examination is no longer routinely recommended in isolation, but women should report any new breast change to their clinician.

Cervical cancer screening with cervical cytology or HPV testing is recommended for women ages 21 to 65. Screening intervals depend on the test used and prior results. Vaccination against human papillomavirus is recommended starting at age 11 to 12 and is approved for ages 9 to 45. Combined screening and vaccination has substantially reduced cervical cancer incidence in countries with established programs.

Air quality alerts are issued when particulate matter or ground-level ozone exceeds health-protective thresholds. Sensitive groups including children, older adults, and people with heart or lung disease should limit prolonged outdoor exertion on alert days. Public health agencies provide real-time air quality indices and forecasts through their websites and dedicated mobile applications.

Heat-related illness is preventable. During hot weather, drink fluids before feeling thirsty, avoid prolonged outdoor activity during peak heat hours, wear lightweight clothing, and never leave children or pets in a parked vehicle. Watch for warning signs of heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, nausea. Heatstroke, indicated by confusion, high body temperature, and absent sweating, is a medical emergency requiring immediate cooling and emergency care.

Carbon monoxide is an odourless, colourless gas produced by combustion. Install battery-powered or battery-backup carbon monoxide detectors near sleeping areas on every level of the home. Have fuel-burning appliances inspected annually. Never run a generator, charcoal grill, or vehicle engine inside a garage or other enclosed space. Symptoms of poisoning include headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, and confusion.

Drinking water in public supply systems is regulated for safety and routinely tested for contaminants. Bottled water is not consistently safer than tap water and contributes to plastic waste. Households served by private wells should test annually for bacteria and every three to five years for chemical contaminants. Filtration may be appropriate for taste, hardness, or specific concerns.

Food safety practices reduce the risk of foodborne illness. Wash hands and surfaces often, separate raw and cooked foods, cook to safe internal temperatures, and refrigerate perishable items promptly. Use a food thermometer to verify cooking temperatures: 63°C for whole cuts of beef, pork, and lamb; 71°C for ground meats; 74°C for poultry. Discard perishable foods left at room temperature longer than two hours.

Workplace hearing protection is required when noise exposure exceeds 85 decibels averaged over an eight-hour shift. Recreational noise above this level, including from concerts, power tools, and personal audio devices, also contributes to permanent hearing loss. Foam ear plugs reduce sound exposure by approximately 25 to 33 decibels when properly inserted. Hearing damage from noise is cumulative and irreversible.

Bicycle helmets reduce the risk of head injury in cycling crashes by approximately 60%. Helmets should fit snugly, sit level on the head, and have a chinstrap that allows no more than two fingers between the strap and the chin. Replace helmets after any impact and approximately every five years regardless of use. Many jurisdictions require helmet use for cyclists under a certain age.

Falls are the leading cause of injury among adults aged 65 and older. Risk factors include muscle weakness, balance problems, vision impairment, medication side effects, and home hazards. Prevention measures include regular strength and balance exercise, medication review, vision checks, removing tripping hazards, installing grab bars in bathrooms, and ensuring adequate lighting on stairs.

Mental health is integral to overall health. Stress, anxiety, and low mood are common, and treatment is effective. Speak with a primary care provider, employer assistance program, or local mental health service about persistent symptoms. Free crisis support is available through national helplines 24 hours a day. Maintaining social connection, regular physical activity, adequate sleep, and structured daily routines all support mental wellbeing.

Routine dental check-ups every six to twelve months allow early detection of caries, gum disease, and oral cancer. Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste for two minutes, floss daily, and limit added sugars to reduce risk of dental decay. Tobacco use, including chewing tobacco, is the leading risk factor for oral cancer.

Eye examinations identify refractive errors and detect early disease such as glaucoma, cataracts, and diabetic retinopathy. Adults aged 40 to 64 should have a comprehensive eye examination at least every two years; adults 65 and older annually. People with diabetes, family history of eye disease, or symptoms such as vision change, eye pain, or new floaters should be evaluated promptly.

Antibiotics treat bacterial infections only; they have no effect on viral illnesses such as the common cold, most sore throats, and influenza. Inappropriate antibiotic use contributes to antimicrobial resistance, a growing public health threat. Take antibiotics exactly as prescribed and complete the full course unless instructed otherwise. Never share or save antibiotics for future use.

Alcohol use guidelines from public health authorities recommend that adults who choose to drink do so in moderation: up to one standard drink per day for women and two for men. There is no level of alcohol consumption that is risk-free. Heavy or binge drinking increases risk of liver disease, several cancers, cardiovascular disease, and injury. Resources for cutting down or stopping are available through primary care and community organisations.

Skin self-checks help identify changes that warrant clinician evaluation. Use the ABCDE rule for new or changing pigmented lesions: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter greater than six millimetres, Evolution over time. Examine the entire body, including areas not exposed to the sun, every few months. Anyone with a personal or family history of skin cancer should also have a periodic clinician skin examination.

Pregnancy planning includes folic acid supplementation, achieving a healthy weight, ensuring vaccinations are up to date, avoiding alcohol and tobacco, and reviewing medications for compatibility with pregnancy. People taking medications for chronic conditions such as epilepsy, diabetes, or hypertension should discuss adjustments with a clinician before conception when possible.

Newborn screening tests every infant for a panel of treatable congenital conditions. The specific panel varies by jurisdiction but typically includes phenylketonuria, congenital hypothyroidism, hearing loss, and several metabolic disorders. Early identification and treatment prevent severe long-term consequences. Results are typically available within a few weeks of birth.

Public health surveillance tracks disease patterns and emerging threats. Reporting of certain infectious diseases is mandatory to permit timely outbreak investigation and response. Surveillance data inform vaccination campaigns, advisories, and resource allocation. Individual reports are kept confidential and used in aggregate to protect community health.

Health system access programs help people without insurance obtain primary and preventive care. Sliding-scale clinics, community health centres, and federally qualified health centres provide care based on ability to pay. Many programs include prescription assistance, mental health services, and dental and vision care. Local health departments can direct individuals to nearby resources.
